subject: Chemistry
title: Chemical Bonding
outline: The octet rule and why atoms combine
Covalent bonding: single, double and triple bonds
Metallic bonding and the electron sea model
Giant covalent structures: diamond, graphite, silica
Van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding

modules.title: 3.1 Why Atoms Combine
modules.html:
Atoms combine in order to attain the stable electron configuration of the nearest noble gas — a duplet (2 electrons, like helium) for the very small atoms, or an octet (8 electrons) for most others. This is the octet rule. The energy of the combined system is lower than that of the separate atoms, so bond formation always releases energy while bond breaking absorbs it.

An atom may achieve stability in three ways:

  • Transfer of electrons — ionic (electrovalent) bonding, typically metal + non-metal.
  • Sharing of electrons, one from each atom — covalent bonding, typically non-metal + non-metal.
  • Donation of a shared pair by one atom only — dative (coordinate) bonding.

Electronegativity difference is the best guide: a difference greater than about 1.7 gives an ionic bond, between 0.4 and 1.7 a polar covalent bond, and below 0.4 a non-polar covalent bond.

examples.q: Why do noble gases rarely form compounds?
examples.a: Their outermost shells already hold a stable octet (or duplet for helium), so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.

examples.q: Predict the bond type in MgCl2 and in CCl4.
examples.a: MgCl2 is ionic (metal and non-metal, large electronegativity difference); CCl4 is covalent (two non-metals with a small difference).

modules.title: 3.2 Electrovalent (Ionic) Bonding
modules.html:
An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the complete transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.

Sodium chloride: \( \mathrm{Na}(2,8,1) \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+}(2,8) + e^- \) and \( \mathrm{Cl}(2,8,7) + e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl^-}(2,8,8) \). The ions attract and pack into a giant cubic lattice in which each Na+ is surrounded by six Cl−.

Magnesium oxide: Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons to O (2,6), giving Mg2+ and O2−. The double charges make the lattice energy very high, so MgO melts at 2852 °C.

Properties of ionic compounds

  • Crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points (strong electrostatic forces throughout the giant lattice).
  • Hard but brittle — a blow shifts the layers so that like charges meet and repel.
  • Generally soluble in water and other polar solvents, insoluble in organic (non-polar) solvents.
  • Conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution (ions become mobile) but not when solid.
  • Reactions between their solutions are fast because they involve only ions.

Ionic bonding is favoured by a metal of low ionisation energy (Group 1 and 2), a non-metal of high electron affinity and electronegativity (Groups 6 and 7), and a high lattice energy.

examples.q: Explain why solid NaCl does not conduct electricity but molten NaCl does.
examples.a: In the solid, ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move. On melting, the lattice collapses and the ions become free to migrate to the electrodes.

examples.q: Why is ionic compound MgO higher melting than NaCl?
examples.a: MgO contains doubly charged Mg2+ and O2− ions; the electrostatic attraction (and lattice energy) is far greater than between singly charged Na+ and Cl−.

modules.title: 3.3 Covalent and Coordinate Bonding
modules.html:
A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons, each atom contributing one. A single bond is one shared pair (H–H, Cl–Cl), a double bond two pairs (O=O, CO2), a triple bond three pairs (N≡N, C2H2).

Examples with dot-and-cross reasoning: H2O (two bonding pairs and two lone pairs on oxygen, bent shape 104.5°), NH3 (three bonding pairs, one lone pair, pyramidal 107°), CH4 (four bonding pairs, tetrahedral 109.5°), CO2 (linear, 180°).

Coordinate (dative) bond

Here both shared electrons come from one atom, the donor, which must possess a lone pair; the acceptor must have an empty orbital. It is shown by an arrow from donor to acceptor.

  • \( \mathrm{NH_3 + H^+ \rightarrow NH_4^+} \) — nitrogen's lone pair is donated to the proton.
  • \( \mathrm{H_2O + H^+ \rightarrow H_3O^+} \) (hydroxonium ion).
  • \( \mathrm{NH_3 + BF_3 \rightarrow H_3N{\rightarrow}BF_3} \) and complex ions such as \( \mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}} \).

Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical in strength and length to an ordinary covalent bond — all four N–H bonds in NH4+ are the same.

Properties of simple covalent (molecular) substances

  • Gases, volatile liquids or soft low-melting solids, because only weak van der Waals forces act between molecules.
  • Do not conduct electricity (no free ions or electrons) — except graphite and molten acids in water.
  • Soluble in organic solvents, usually insoluble in water unless they can hydrogen bond.
  • Reactions are usually slow, since strong covalent bonds must be broken.

Giant covalent (network) solids

Diamond: each carbon is bonded to four others tetrahedrally — extremely hard, very high melting point, non-conductor. Graphite: layers of hexagonal rings, each carbon bonded to three others with one delocalised electron — soft, slippery lubricant and a good conductor. Silicon(IV) oxide has a similar giant structure and is used in glass and sand.

Metallic bonding

Metallic bonding is the attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a "sea" of delocalised valence electrons. This explains why metals conduct heat and electricity, are malleable and ductile (layers slide without breaking the bond), are lustrous, and generally have high melting points and densities.

examples.q: Why is ammonium ion said to contain a dative bond, yet all its bonds are identical?
examples.a: Nitrogen supplies both electrons for the fourth bond when it accepts H+, but once formed that bond is indistinguishable in length and strength from the other three N–H covalent bonds.

examples.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not.
examples.a: In graphite each carbon uses only three of its four valence electrons in bonding; the fourth is delocalised between layers and free to move. In diamond all four are locked in covalent bonds.

modules.title: 3.4 Intermolecular Forces
modules.html:
Forces between molecules are far weaker than the covalent bonds within them, but they decide melting point, boiling point, solubility and viscosity.

Van der Waals (dispersion) forces

Momentary uneven distribution of electrons creates a temporary dipole that induces dipoles in neighbours. They are weak but increase with molecular size and surface area — this is why the boiling points of the halogens rise F2 < Cl2 < Br2 < I2, and why the alkanes become less volatile as the chain lengthens.

Dipole–dipole attraction

In polar molecules such as HCl, the permanent partial charges (δ+ on H, δ− on Cl) attract neighbouring molecules, raising the boiling point above that of a non-polar molecule of similar mass.

Hydrogen bonding

A specially strong dipole attraction occurs when hydrogen is bonded to the small, highly electronegative atoms fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N in another molecule. Consequences:

  • Water boils at 100 °C, far above H2S (−60 °C), despite its smaller molar mass.
  • Ice is less dense than water because hydrogen bonding holds molecules in an open tetrahedral network — so ice floats and aquatic life survives.
  • Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity, surface tension and latent heat of vaporisation.
  • Ethanol, ammonia, carboxylic acids and sugars are very soluble in water; carboxylic acids form dimers in non-polar solvents.
  • Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands of DNA and shape proteins.

Order of strength: ionic/covalent bonds (≈400 kJ mol⁻¹) > hydrogen bonds (≈20–40) > dipole–dipole > van der Waals (≈1–10 kJ mol⁻¹).

examples.q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide?
examples.a: Water molecules are linked by strong hydrogen bonds (O is small and very electronegative), which need much more energy to break than the weak dipole forces between H2S molecules.

examples.q: Why do the boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group?
examples.a: Larger atoms have more electrons and are more polarisable, so van der Waals forces become stronger.

quiz.q: Atoms combine chiefly in order to
options: attain a stable noble gas configuration
quiz.solution: Stability of the duplet or octet drives bonding.

quiz.q: An electrovalent bond is formed by
quiz.solution: Complete transfer produces oppositely charged ions.

quiz.q: Ionic bonding usually occurs between
quiz.solution: Low ionisation energy metal plus high electronegativity non-metal.

quiz.q: In NaCl the sodium ion has the configuration
quiz.solution: Na loses its 3s electron to become 2,8 like neon.

quiz.q: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when
quiz.solution: Ions must be mobile to carry charge.

quiz.q: Ionic compounds generally have high melting points because
options: of the strong electrostatic forces in the giant lattice
quiz.solution: Much energy is needed to overcome the lattice attractions.

quiz.q: Magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride because
quiz.solution: Higher ionic charges give a much larger lattice energy.

quiz.q: A covalent bond is formed when atoms
quiz.solution: Each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair.

quiz.q: The number of shared pairs in a nitrogen molecule N2 is
quiz.solution: N≡N is a triple bond.

quiz.q: Which molecule contains a double bond?
quiz.solution: O=O contains two shared pairs.

quiz.q: The shape of a methane molecule is
quiz.solution: Four bonding pairs repel to 109.5°.

quiz.q: The shape of the ammonia molecule is
quiz.solution: The lone pair on nitrogen pushes the three N–H bonds into a pyramid.

quiz.q: The bond angle in water is approximately
quiz.solution: Two lone pairs compress the H–O–H angle to about 104.5°.

quiz.q: A dative bond differs from a normal covalent bond in that
options: both electrons come from one atom
quiz.solution: The donor supplies the whole shared pair.

quiz.q: Which species contains a coordinate bond?
quiz.solution: Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+.

quiz.q: The hydroxonium ion is formed when
quiz.solution: H2O + H+ → H3O+ using a lone pair on oxygen.

quiz.q: In the complex [Cu(NH3)4]2+ the ammonia molecules act as
quiz.solution: Each NH3 donates a lone pair to the copper ion.

quiz.q: Metallic bonding is best described as
options: sharing of pairs between two atoms
attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
quiz.solution: The electron sea model explains metallic properties.

quiz.q: Metals are malleable because
options: layers of ions can slide without breaking the metallic bond
quiz.solution: The delocalised electrons keep holding the sliding layers together.

quiz.q: Diamond is very hard because
options: each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network
quiz.solution: A giant covalent network resists deformation.

quiz.q: Graphite is used as a lubricant because
options: its layers slide over one another
quiz.solution: Weak forces between hexagonal layers allow sliding.

quiz.q: Which allotrope of carbon conducts electricity?
quiz.solution: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom.

quiz.q: Simple covalent substances have low melting points because
options: the forces between molecules are weak
quiz.solution: Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome, not the covalent bonds.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT conduct electricity in any state?
quiz.solution: Sulphur is a simple covalent solid with neither ions nor free electrons.

quiz.q: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is bonded to
quiz.solution: F, O and N are small and highly electronegative.

quiz.q: Ice floats on water because
options: hydrogen bonding creates an open structure in ice
quiz.solution: The open tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded lattice makes ice less dense.

quiz.q: The boiling points of halogens increase down the group because
options: van der Waals forces increase with molecular size
quiz.solution: Larger, more polarisable molecules attract more strongly.

quiz.q: The weakest of these forces is
quiz.solution: Dispersion forces are only a few kJ per mole.

quiz.q: A bond with electronegativity difference of 2.1 is best described as
quiz.solution: Differences above about 1.7 give ionic character.

quiz.q: HCl has a higher boiling point than F2 of similar mass mainly because HCl
options: is polar and has dipole–dipole forces
quiz.solution: Permanent dipoles attract more strongly than dispersion forces alone.

quiz.q: Which compound is soluble in water because of hydrogen bonding?
quiz.solution: Ethanol's –OH group hydrogen bonds with water.

quiz.q: Bond formation is always
quiz.solution: Energy is released as the more stable bonded state forms.

quiz.q: The maximum number of covalent bonds normally formed by carbon is
quiz.solution: Carbon has four valence electrons.

quiz.q: Ionic compounds are usually insoluble in
quiz.solution: Non-polar organic solvents cannot solvate ions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a giant covalent structure?
quiz.solution: SiO2 forms a continuous covalent network.

quiz.q: The particles present in a metallic crystal are
quiz.solution: Metal cations sit in a sea of mobile electrons.

quiz.q: The bond in a chlorine molecule is
quiz.solution: Identical atoms share the pair equally.

quiz.q: Ionic crystals are brittle because
options: displaced layers bring like charges together, causing repulsion
quiz.solution: A blow shifts one layer and like charges repel, splitting the crystal.

quiz.q: In NH4+ how many of the N–H bonds are dative?
quiz.solution: Only the bond formed by donating the lone pair is dative in origin.

quiz.q: Which one has the strongest intermolecular forces?
quiz.solution: Water has extensive hydrogen bonding.

quiz.q: An element with 2 valence electrons will most likely form
quiz.solution: Losing two electrons gives a stable octet.

quiz.q: Which pair forms an ionic compound?
quiz.solution: A Group 1 metal with a Group 7 non-metal.

quiz.q: Substances with giant covalent structures are usually
quiz.solution: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

quiz.q: The dative bond in NH3→BF3 is possible because BF3 has
quiz.solution: Boron has only six electrons and an empty orbital to accept a pair.

quiz.q: Which property is NOT typical of ionic compounds?
quiz.solution: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct.

quiz.q: Delocalised electrons in metals explain their
quiz.solution: Mobile electrons carry current.

quiz.q: Carboxylic acids dimerise in non-polar solvents because of
quiz.solution: Two molecules pair through two O–H⋯O hydrogen bonds.

quiz.q: The strength of a hydrogen bond is roughly
quiz.solution: Hydrogen bonds are intermediate in strength.

quiz.q: Which molecule is non-polar despite having polar bonds?
quiz.solution: CO2 is linear so the two bond dipoles cancel.

quiz.q: The type of bonding in solid iodine is covalent within molecules and ____ between molecules.
quiz.solution: Iodine is a simple molecular solid held by dispersion forces.
